result:
There is a specific kind of magic that happens to a city after midnight when it begins to rain. The daytime chaos of honking horns, hurried footsteps, and relentless chatter dissolves into a rhythmic, soothing hiss. Ordinary asphalt transforms into black glass, catching the bleed of neon signs and traffic lights, turning shallow puddles into shimmering portals of crimson, amber, and electric blue.

Standing by a window during these hours feels like existing entirely outside of time. The vast world shrinks to the size of your room and the immediate halo of the streetlamp below. Tires whisper against the wet pavement as a lone taxi glides past, carrying someone home from a late shift or away from a lingering goodbye. In the daylight, solitude can sometimes ache like loneliness, sharp and demanding. At two in the morning, however, solitude softens into sanctuary, because nobody expects anything from you while the world sleeps.

Look across the skyline, and you will always spot a few illuminated squares scattered across dark apartment buildings. They belong to fellow insomniacs, restless thinkers, artists chasing a fleeting spark, or new parents pacing the wooden floorboards. There is an unspoken camaraderie among everyone awake in the small hours, united by the steady percussion against the glass.

Soon, the dark sky will bruise into dawn. Alarms will ring, coffee will brew, and streets will dry into ordinary gray stone. Until that moment arrives, the quiet city belongs entirely to the silver rain and the dreamers watching it fall.
